strengths: Originality: The frozen-multiplier Lagrangian combined with linearized active constraints is a useful construction. Under suitable local regularity, the KKT comparison in Appendix B explains how it preserves solution sensitivity while enabling equality-constrained finite differences.

Significance: Solver-independent differentiation is practically valuable. Section 5’s use of the detached incoming gradient as a linear perturbation provides a clear way to integrate the method into automatic differentiation.

Empirical merits: The experiments cover synthetic QPs, Sudoku, and a nonlinear constrained problem, with several relevant baselines. Training curves suggest comparable optimization performance, and the tolerance, gradient-error, and GPU comparisons provide useful additional evidence.

Presentation and responsible scope: The main algorithm and implementation interface are understandable. Appendix F explicitly examines the active-set assumption, and Appendix D acknowledges difficulties with general convex constraints. The impact statement is proportionate; no material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—main theorem assumptions are insufficient. Theorem 4.6 invokes only Assumptions 4.2–4.3, whereas its supporting equivalence theorem additionally requires differentiability and a locally constant active set. Correctly identifying the active set does not ensure either property at a switching point. Moreover, Lemma C.1 derives O(δ²) Taylor remainders from twice-continuous differentiability and differentiability of the solution path, which do not generally imply those remainder bounds. The claimed O(δ) bias requires stronger quantitative regularity. Appendix A also uses an undefined Hessian-smoothness constant Sg absent from Assumption 4.2.

Soundness—the advertised general-convex first-order complexity is not established. Theorem C.2 asserts that the original and perturbed problems are well-conditioned and therefore solvable to O(ϵ²) accuracy in logarithmic time, without specifying a first-order algorithm establishing this for the original nonlinear constrained problem. Appendix D.1 explicitly acknowledges the missing dual-convergence algorithm and instead assumes an approximate primal-dual solution oracle with correct active constraints. Complexity measured in calls to this stronger oracle does not establish the main text’s general O(log(1/ϵ)) gradient-oracle claim.

The inexact-gradient proof contains a consequential dual-recovery error. In Theorem C.2, the reconstructed perturbed multiplier uses only ∇y g̃, omitting δ∇y f; its sign also conflicts with the stated KKT convention. Even with an exact perturbed primal solution, omitting this term can introduce O(δ) multiplier error, rather than the asserted O(ϵ²) error. Division by δ in the estimator can therefore leave nonvanishing error. The proof needs a corrected reconstruction and complete error propagation.

The scalability interpretation exceeds the evidence. The complexity analysis concerns accuracy, not dimension, and cannot justify Section 7’s claim that backpropagation cost grows sublinearly with problem size. Runtime comparisons also mix solver backends and canonicalization costs; much of the observed advantage occurs in the forward pass. Matched-backend comparisons and a specified FFOQP backward implementation are needed to isolate the differentiation method’s contribution. The three small benchmark families provide promising evidence, but do not establish broad robustness to ill-conditioning.

The memory results require reconciliation. Figures 6–7 report approximately 400–500 GB for CvxpyLayer, although Appendix G.1 describes a 384 GB allocation. Appendix G.2 calls these GPU-memory measurements despite the main experiments being described as CPU runs. Measurements are also plotted at dimension 1000 while Figure 5 reports out-of-memory there. Units, measurement procedures, hardware, and treatment of failed runs are necessary to assess this central scalability claim.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Appendix G.1 gives seed counts and dataset size but omits actual learning rates, batch sizes, network widths, problem-generation distributions, the perturbation magnitude, and active-set thresholds. LPGD’s tolerance is described inconsistently: Section 7 says it matches the proposed method, while Appendix G reports tightening it to 10⁻¹². These details materially affect both accuracy and timing. The useful idea and encouraging experiments do not outweigh the unresolved theoretical and evidential gaps.

strengths: Significance: Efficient differentiation through constrained optimization is an important problem. A solver-independent backward pass could make established convex solvers easier to integrate into learning pipelines.

Originality: The frozen-multiplier Lagrangian combined with linearized active constraints is a useful construction. Under suitable regularity and active-set stability, the KKT comparison in Appendix B provides a convincing explanation of why the surrogate preserves local sensitivity.

Methodology and presentation: Replacing the upper-level loss by its detached linearization gives a practical way to implement vector–Jacobian products using the incoming gradient. Sections 4–5 explain this connection clearly.

Empirical merits: The evaluation includes synthetic QPs, Sudoku, and nonlinear convex constraints, with several relevant baselines. Training curves support comparable optimization behavior on these examples, and the tolerance, gradient-agreement, and GPU-baseline ablations add useful evidence.

Limitations and ethics: Appendices D and F explicitly discuss difficulties with nonlinear constraints and active-set identification. These discussions are valuable. The impact statement is proportionate to the methodological contribution, and I see no material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness—main theorem assumptions are insufficient. Theorem 4.5 requires differentiability and a locally constant active set, but Theorem 4.6 invokes only Assumptions 4.2–4.3. Correctly identifying the active set does not ensure either property. For example, g(x,y)=(y−x)^2/2, h(x,y)=−y, and f(x,y)=y satisfy the stated smoothness, strong-convexity, and LICQ conditions, yet F(x)=max(x,0) has no gradient at zero. The pointwise guarantee therefore needs qualification, and the outer convergence result needs an explicit argument handling exceptional points and uniform oracle bounds.

Soundness—finite-difference accuracy and inexact solves are not adequately established. Lemma C.1 assumes twice-continuous differentiability and a differentiable solution map, then uses O(δ²) Taylor remainders in Equation 19; these assumptions alone do not justify that rate. Appropriate Lipschitz derivative assumptions are needed. Moreover, Theorem C.2's reconstructed perturbed multiplier omits the δ∇y f term required by perturbed stationarity, as well as the sign under the stated KKT convention. This omission can produce O(δ) multiplier error, which becomes O(1) after division by δ. These issues directly affect the advertised ε-accurate oracle.

Soundness and significance—the general-convex complexity claim counts a substantially stronger oracle. Assumption D.1 supplies approximate primal and dual solutions with the correct active set, and the authors explicitly state that they do not know an algorithm with the required linear dual convergence. Consequently, Corollary D.5 is conditional on this solver oracle; it does not establish the broadly advertised first-order gradient complexity for general convex constraints. Theorem C.2 also asserts that the original constrained problem is well-conditioned and quickly solvable without supplying the requisite first-order algorithm and complexity conditions.

Empirical support—the runtime comparisons do not isolate the proposed differentiation mechanism. Methods use different backends and canonicalization paths, and Section 7 attributes substantial gains to forward-pass implementation differences. The QP specialization's closed-form backward computation is insufficiently specified. Matched-backend comparisons at matched solution and gradient accuracy are needed to establish which gains come from the new oracle.

Scalability claims exceed the evidence. The complexity analysis concerns accuracy dependence, not sublinear dependence on problem dimension, yet Section 7 claims the latter follows from the theory. Figure 5 does not establish this scaling. Memory reporting also contains unresolved inconsistencies: Appendix G.2 calls the measurements GPU memory despite the stated CPU setup, and Figures 6–7 report roughly 500 GB despite a stated 384 GB allocation. The measurement procedure, units, and treatment of failed runs require clarification.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the implementation claims. The manuscript's code-availability sentence provides no usable link. Appendix G does not specify numerical learning rates, default batch sizes, perturbation magnitudes, active-set thresholds, complete synthetic-instance generation, or the precise FFOQP backend and backward procedure. Ten seeds are reported, but the main runtime comparisons do not quantify uncertainty.

Presentation and originality positioning need tightening. Recasting a differentiable layer as bilevel optimization and perturbing the objective are established ideas; the contribution should be centered on the active-set surrogate and its validated guarantees. Claims of superior robustness to ill-conditioning lack controlled conditioning experiments, and the broad description of implicit methods as requiring Hessian inversion overlooks iterative linear-system approaches. These overstatements obscure the narrower contribution that the manuscript does support.

strengths: Originality: The useful methodological contribution is the active-set Lagrangian surrogate: freezing multipliers while linearizing active constraints preserves constraint curvature through the objective. Theorem 4.5 provides a plausible local equivalence argument under its stated regularity and active-set stability conditions.

Significance: Solver-independent differentiation through an additional perturbed optimization problem could make optimization layers easier to integrate and scale. The incoming-gradient linearization in Section 5 is a practical way to implement the backward pass without requiring the downstream loss inside the solver.

Evaluation: The paper compares several relevant baselines across synthetic QP, Sudoku, and SOCP tasks. Training curves, separate forward/backward timings, ten random seeds, and additional tolerance, GPU, and gradient-comparison experiments provide useful preliminary evidence.

Presentation and limitations: The main construction is explained clearly. Appendices D and F explicitly discuss difficulties with nonlinear constraints and active-set identification, and the impact statement appropriately acknowledges downstream application risks. I see no material research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: Soundness—central guarantees exceed their assumptions. Theorem 4.6 assumes only Assumptions 4.2–4.3, whereas its supporting equivalence theorem additionally requires differentiability and a locally constant active set. Correct active-set identification does not imply either. For example, minimizing (y−x)^2/2 subject to y≥0 with f(x,y)=y satisfies smoothness, strong convexity, and LICQ, but F(x)=max(x,0) has no gradient at zero. The claimed pointwise hypergradient guarantee therefore cannot hold as stated. The Goldstein-stationarity result needs a precise argument establishing where the oracle applies and the required uniform bounds.

Soundness—finite-difference accuracy is insufficiently justified. Lemma C.1 assumes twice-continuously differentiable functions and differentiability of the primal-dual solution path, then asserts O(δ²) Taylor remainders in Equation 19. Those assumptions alone do not establish these remainders or the resulting O(δ) bias; stronger quantitative regularity is needed. Assumption 4.2 is weaker still. Appendix A also uses an undefined Hessian-smoothness constant Sg. These gaps directly affect the perturbation choice and advertised accuracy complexity.

Soundness and scope—the general-convex first-order complexity claim is not established. Theorem C.2 asserts that the original constrained problem can be solved to the required accuracy in logarithmic time without specifying and analyzing a suitable first-order solver. Appendix D.1 instead assumes an approximate primal-dual solution oracle and explicitly distinguishes its oracle complexity from gradient complexity. That conditional result is useful, but it does not establish the broadly advertised logarithmic first-order cost for general convex constraints. The proof also needs to account explicitly for errors in the frozen multipliers and linearized constraints.

Experimental validity: The scalability interpretation is substantially stronger than the evidence. Accuracy-oracle complexity does not imply sublinear runtime in decision dimension, as claimed in Section 7; per-oracle costs and conditioning remain relevant. Figure 7 labels measurements as GPU memory despite the stated CPU setup, while Figures 6–7 report approximately 500 GB against a stated 384 GB allocation. The nearly identical initialization, forward, and backward memory curves require an explanation of the measurement procedure. Backend and canonicalization differences also confound attributing the reported speedups specifically to first-order differentiation.

Reproducibility: Important settings are missing, including the finite-difference perturbation used experimentally, active-set thresholds, the FFOQP backward implementation and selected qpsolvers backend, numerical learning rates and batch sizes, and sufficient details of synthetic problem generation. The abstract's source-code availability sentence contains no link in the supplied manuscript. These omissions are particularly consequential because performance and accuracy depend on solver tolerances and active-set decisions.

Evidence for robustness remains limited. Figure 11 shows cosine similarity falling toward 0.5 in some configurations, but provides no relative-gradient-error analysis or controlled accuracy-versus-perturbation study. Training-loss agreement alone does not validate the claimed hypergradient accuracy or robustness to ill-conditioning. Controlled conditioning and active-set-transition experiments, together with matched-backend comparisons, would materially strengthen the contribution. Overall, the promising construction and preliminary results do not outweigh the unresolved gaps in the central theoretical and scalability claims.
